Nelson City Council has formally adopted its Annual Plan 2026/27, retaining the forecast average rates increase of 4.7%. 

The Annual Plan was adopted at a Council meeting on Thursday 25 June, confirming it will proceed without significant changes from Year Three of the Long Term Plan 2024-34. 

Nelson Mayor Nick Smith says keeping the average rates increase to 4.7% is a significant achievement for Council. 

“This 4.7% rise is well below the average rate increase around the country of about 8%. It is also well down on the 6.5% increase last year and 8.2% increase the previous year. This is the first time we have got to Year Three of a Long Term Plan and been able to adopt an Annual Plan without consultation, while sticking closely to what we had already consulted on, which is a saving in both time and money, and upholds the integrity of the Long Term Plan process. 

“It is easy giving speeches of concern about cost-of-living pressures but so much harder to keep costs such as rates down. Council is facing all the same cost pressures as households and businesses, and it has taken a huge effort, particularly by Council staff, to keep this year’s rate increase to a minimum.” 

In the Annual Plan, Council has also agreed to keep the proportion of commercial rates at 22.3%, the same as in 2025/26. 

Transport budgets have been updated to reflect additional NZTA Waka Kotahi funding for resilience projects, with some other transport projects reprioritised. Stormwater projects, including York Terrace and Tāhunanui Catchment 9, have been adjusted to align with revised design and construction timing. Funding has also been carried forward for Maitai resilience projects. 

Mayor Nick says the Annual Plan also supports projects that will help build confidence in Nelson’s future. 

“The resilience work in the Maitai is a big project of which we can be proud. We all want to see our city revitalised, and the massive investment in our city through Bridge to Better, alongside private-sector investment such as the Safari Group development, is the dividend of Council being bold and investing in Nelson’s future. 

“I acknowledge that for businesses and households it is hard going right now, but I am increasingly confident about Nelson’s economic recovery. Our city has never had such a strong pipeline of projects. The combination of Bridge to Better, Morrison Square, the Safari Group central-city development, Maitahi residential development, five big affordable housing projects and the Nelson Hospital redevelopment pave the way for a strong recovery over the next three years.”

The RNZ site at Saxton Field will be vested as a reserve for public recreation, following a joint purchase by Nelson City Council and Tasman District Council - Te Kaunihera o te tai o Aorere.

RNZ retired its ageing AM radio transmitter site at Stoke in late March 2025, as it had become surplus to requirements with other RNZ radio frequencies serving the Nelson Tasman region.

Purchasing this land at Saxton Field secures another 7.14 hectares of one of the region's busiest spots for sport and recreation.

The space includes playing fields, carparking, a playground with shade sails and a concrete shared path, along with roading, drainage, street and sports lighting, established trees and a sand storage facility. The transmission building on the site will stay and be put to use for the reserve.

Nelson Mayor Nick Smith welcomed the agreement reached between the two councils and RNZ.

“I’m delighted our two councils have been able to conclude the purchase of this central 7.14 hectares of land from RNZ,” Mayor Nick said.

“Saxton Field is one of the best sports and recreation facilities in the country, but it would have been gutted if this central block was lost to developers.

“The two councils and RNZ are all under financial pressure, but with goodwill, we have been able to come to a price that is fair to all. I acknowledge and thank RNZ for allowing us to use and develop the area around the radio mast for the past 40 years, and for enabling us to secure the area as a permanent public recreation reserve.”

Joint Saxton Field Committee Chair Councillor Campbell Rollo welcomed the joint purchase.

“Saxton Field is the heart of sport and recreation for our region, and acquiring this land ensures it is protected for future generations. It provides certainty for the families, sports clubs, and visitors who use the reserve every week,” Councillor Rollo said.

“Working alongside Tasman District Council to secure this land is a practical and sensible approach to looking after a reserve that is valued and shared by both communities."

Something shifted over in Kaiteriteri a few weeks ago.

Eighty people walked into a room as strangers: volunteers, scientists, landowners, and community group members from right across Te Tauihu. A regional trapping hui that was, on paper, about pest control techniques turned into something far more powerful: proof that Nelson and Tasman's conservation community is alive, growing, and ready for more hands.

Imagine walking the Maitai track on an ordinary Tuesday morning and hearing a korimako/bellbird call from the canopy. Watching piwakawaka/fantails dart through your garden not as a rare treat, but as an everyday thing. Knowing that the bush behind your kid's school is genuinely recovering because of what people in your community are doing now. 

Darren Peters, who has watched trapping evolve from gutfeel to science-backed practice over many years, reminded the room that the most effective programmes stay adaptable. 

Dr Graeme Elliott brought research straight from the field, sharing what careful monitoring of banded rail along our coastline is telling us about how best we can protect this threatened species. 

Between presentations, people compared notes. The programme featured a mix of presentations and hands-on workshops, covering topics such as pest animal behaviour, effective trapping techniques, monitoring methods and the use of tools like Trap.NZ. 

Emerging technologies for large-scale and remote projects were also explored alongside practical insights participants could take back to their own programmes. 

The hui also covered the challenges. Keeping volunteers energised over the long haul is genuinely difficult. Younger people aren't always finding their way in. Some landowners remain hard to reach, funding is a challenge, and the information that proves conservation outcomes isn't always being collected consistently enough to tell the full story. 

And yet, what stood out most strongly was that no one needs to tackle these challenges alone.

The hui underscored something simple but powerful: conservation in our region is driven by connection. People left not just with new knowledge, but with new relationships. 

Sharing ideas, comparing approaches, and seeing what others are achieving reinforced the value of working collectively and the strength of the volunteer network behind much of this work.

As one participant reflected, “I was really inspired by the passion and creativity people bring to this work, everyone is genuinely doing their best to help our native ecosystems thrive.”

The hui was made possible by Te Tauihu Environment Trust (TET), with support from Predator Free New Zealand Trust, Department of Conservation (DOC), Nelson City Council and Tasman District Council - Te Kaunihera o te tai o Aorere. 

To learn more about trapping in our region, contact nelson.nature@ncc.govt.nz or sign up to TET’s newsletter via their website.

    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">Council confirms 4.7% rates increase 

Nelson City Council has formally adopted its Annual Plan 2026/27, retaining the forecast average rates increase of 4.7%. 

The Annual Plan was adopted at a Council meeting on Thursday 25 June, confirming it will proceed without significant changes from Year Three of the Long Term Plan 2024-34. 

Nelson Mayor Nick Smith says keeping the average rates increase to 4.7% is a significant achievement for Council. 

“This 4.7% rise is well below the average rate increase around the country of about 8%. It is also well down on the 6.5% increase last year and 8.2% increase the previous year. This is the first time we have got to Year Three of a Long Term Plan and been able to adopt an Annual Plan without consultation, while sticking closely to what we had already consulted on, which is a saving in both time and money, and upholds the integrity of the Long Term Plan process. 

“It is easy giving speeches of concern about cost-of-living pressures but so much harder to keep costs such as rates down. Council is facing all the same cost pressures as households and businesses, and it has taken a huge effort, particularly by Council staff, to keep this year’s rate increase to a minimum.” 

In the Annual Plan, Council has also agreed to keep the proportion of commercial rates at 22.3%, the same as in 2025/26. 

Transport budgets have been updated to reflect additional NZTA Waka Kotahi funding for resilience projects, with some other transport projects reprioritised. Stormwater projects, including York Terrace and Tāhunanui Catchment 9, have been adjusted to align with revised design and construction timing. Funding has also been carried forward for Maitai resilience projects. 

Mayor Nick says the Annual Plan also supports projects that will help build confidence in Nelson’s future. 

“The resilience work in the Maitai is a big project of which we can be proud. We all want to see our city revitalised, and the massive investment in our city through Bridge to Better, alongside private-sector investment such as the Safari Group development, is the dividend of Council being bold and investing in Nelson’s future. 

“I acknowledge that for businesses and households it is hard going right now, but I am increasingly confident about Nelson’s economic recovery. Our city has never had such a strong pipeline of projects. The combination of Bridge to Better, Morrison Square, the Safari Group central-city development, Maitahi residential development, five big affordable housing projects and the Nelson Hospital redevelopment pave the way for a strong recovery over the next three years.” 

The final Annual Plan 2026/27 will be published online and made available at Council’s Customer Service Centre and local libraries from mid-July 2026. </p>

    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">Councils purchase RNZ site at Saxton Field

The <a class="link" href="https://nz.linkedin.com/company/rnznewzealand?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>RNZ</a> site at Saxton Field will be vested as a reserve for public recreation, following a joint purchase by <a class="link" href="https://nz.linkedin.com/company/nelson-city-council?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>Nelson City Council</a> and <a class="link" href="https://nz.linkedin.com/company/tasmandistrictcouncil?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>Tasman District Council - Te Kaunihera o te tai o Aorere</a>.

RNZ retired its ageing AM radio transmitter site at Stoke in late March 2025, as it had become surplus to requirements with other RNZ radio frequencies serving the Nelson Tasman region.

Purchasing this land at Saxton Field secures another 7.14 hectares of one of the region's busiest spots for sport and recreation.

The space includes playing fields, carparking, a playground with shade sails and a concrete shared path, along with roading, drainage, street and sports lighting, established trees and a sand storage facility. The transmission building on the site will stay and be put to use for the reserve.

Nelson Mayor Nick Smith welcomed the agreement reached between the two councils and RNZ.

“I’m delighted our two councils have been able to conclude the purchase of this central 7.14 hectares of land from RNZ,” Mayor Nick said.

“Saxton Field is one of the best sports and recreation facilities in the country, but it would have been gutted if this central block was lost to developers.

“The two councils and RNZ are all under financial pressure, but with goodwill, we have been able to come to a price that is fair to all. I acknowledge and thank RNZ for allowing us to use and develop the area around the radio mast for the past 40 years, and for enabling us to secure the area as a permanent public recreation reserve.”

Joint Saxton Field Committee Chair Councillor Campbell Rollo welcomed the joint purchase.

“Saxton Field is the heart of sport and recreation for our region, and acquiring this land ensures it is protected for future generations. It provides certainty for the families, sports clubs, and visitors who use the reserve every week,” Councillor Rollo said.

“Working alongside Tasman District Council to secure this land is a practical and sensible approach to looking after a reserve that is valued and shared by both communities."

    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">The quiet army protecting our backyard.

Something shifted over in Kaiteriteri a few weeks ago.

Eighty people walked into a room as strangers: volunteers, scientists, landowners, and community group members from right across Te Tauihu. A regional trapping hui that was, on paper, about pest control techniques turned into something far more powerful: proof that Nelson and Tasman's conservation community is alive, growing, and ready for more hands.

Imagine walking the Maitai track on an ordinary Tuesday morning and hearing a korimako/bellbird call from the canopy. Watching piwakawaka/fantails dart through your garden not as a rare treat, but as an everyday thing. Knowing that the bush behind your kid's school is genuinely recovering because of what people in your community are doing now. 

Darren Peters, who has watched trapping evolve from gutfeel to science-backed practice over many years, reminded the room that the most effective programmes stay adaptable. 

Dr Graeme Elliott brought research straight from the field, sharing what careful monitoring of banded rail along our coastline is telling us about how best we can protect this threatened species. 

Between presentations, people compared notes. The programme featured a mix of presentations and hands-on workshops, covering topics such as pest animal behaviour, effective trapping techniques, monitoring methods and the use of tools like <a class="link" href="http://Trap.NZ?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" rel="nofollow" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>Trap.NZ</a>. 

Emerging technologies for large-scale and remote projects were also explored alongside practical insights participants could take back to their own programmes. 

The hui also covered the challenges. Keeping volunteers energised over the long haul is genuinely difficult. Younger people aren't always finding their way in. Some landowners remain hard to reach, funding is a challenge, and the information that proves conservation outcomes isn't always being collected consistently enough to tell the full story. 

And yet, what stood out most strongly was that no one needs to tackle these challenges alone.

The hui underscored something simple but powerful: conservation in our region is driven by connection. People left not just with new knowledge, but with new relationships. 

Sharing ideas, comparing approaches, and seeing what others are achieving reinforced the value of working collectively and the strength of the volunteer network behind much of this work.

As one participant reflected, “I was really inspired by the passion and creativity people bring to this work, everyone is genuinely doing their best to help our native ecosystems thrive.”

The hui was made possible by <a class="link" href="https://nz.linkedin.com/company/te-tauihu-environment-trust?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>Te Tauihu Environment Trust</a> (TET), with support from <a class="link" href="https://nz.linkedin.com/company/predatorfreenz?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>Predator Free New Zealand Trust</a>, <a class="link" href="https://nz.linkedin.com/company/docgovtnz?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>Department of Conservation (DOC)</a>, <a class="link" href="https://nz.linkedin.com/company/nelson-city-council?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>Nelson City Council</a> and <a class="link" href="https://nz.linkedin.com/company/tasmandistrictcouncil?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>Tasman District Council - Te Kaunihera o te tai o Aorere</a>.
